verdicts.evidence: https://pypi.org/pypi/lgpio/json (fetched 2026-10-08): releases are only 0.0.0.2, 0.1.0.0 and 0.2.2.0. 0.2.2.0 has 12 wheels uploaded 2024-03-29 to 2024-04-13: cp39/cp310/cp311/cp312 x (linux_armv7l, manylinux_2_34_aarch64, manylinux_2_34_x86_64), plus the sdist (13 files). No cp313+ wheel. The sdist (https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/source/l/lgpio/lgpio-0.2.2.0.tar.gz) contains lgpio.i, lgpio_extra.py and src/*.c|h, but no generated *_wrap.c and no lgpio.py. setup.py says 'The package's module lgpio.py is produced by SWIG'. With PYPI=1 it builds 'a statically linked module that incorporates the liblgpio library': sources=src/lg*.c + ['lgpio.i','src/rgpiod.c'], libraries=['rt','dl']. Otherwise it builds 'a dynamically linked module': sources=['lgpio.i'], libraries=['lgpio']. So SWIG, a C compiler and Python headers are needed. Caveat: 'builds from the sdist' holds for PyPI-only installs. On 32-bit Pi OS, pip's default piwheels index serves a cp313 armv7l wheel instead (see IMG-06).

verdicts.corrected_claim: piwheels has wheels for cp311 and cp313 on linux_armv7l and linux_armv6l only (32-bit) for lgpio 0.2.2.0, gpiod 2.5.0, uvloop 0.23.0, httptools 0.8.0 and websockets 17.2. Its FAQ says it 'does not currently support the 64-bit version of the Raspberry Pi OS' and lists Bookworm (Python 3.11) and Trixie (Python 3.13). The piwheels lgpio cp313 wheels are dynamically linked: their apt dependencies are libc6 and liblgpio1. So they work only where Raspberry Pi's liblgpio1 is installed, as it is on Pi OS Trixie, and fail in a plain Debian or python container image. On 64-bit Trixie (aarch64, cp313), neither PyPI nor piwheels has an lgpio wheel. The prebuilt options are Raspberry Pi's apt package python3-lgpio and third-party, statically linked lgpio 0.2.2.0 wheels for cp313, cp314 and cp315 linux_aarch64 from Adafruit's adafruit/lgpio-python-wheels GitHub repo, installed with --find-links.
verdicts.evidence: https://www.piwheels.org/project/{lgpio,gpiod,uvloop,httptools,websockets}/json/ : each version has exactly 4 wheels, cp311/cp313 x linux_armv6l/linux_armv7l. For lgpio-0.2.2.0-cp313-cp313-linux_armv7l.whl and the armv6l wheel, apt_dependencies is ['libc6', 'liblgpio1']. https://www.piwheels.org/faq.html: 'The repository at piwheels.org does not currently support the 64-bit version of the Raspberry Pi OS. We have plans to support it in future...' and '...Bullseye - Python 3.9 (end-of-life) Bookworm - Python 3.11 Trixie - Python 3.13'. This refutes 'no prebuilt wheel anywhere': https://github.com/adafruit/lgpio-python-wheels describes itself as 'lgpio wheels for Python 3.13 and later'. Its wheels are cp313/cp314/cp315 Linux ARM64, 'statically linked and self-contained — no system libraries or build tools needed', built with PYPI=1, and installed with 'pip install lgpio --find-links https://github.com/adafruit/lgpio-python-wheels/raw/main/wheels/'. HEAD on .../wheels/lgpio-0.2.2.0-cp313-cp313-linux_aarch64.whl returns HTTP 200, 376,845 bytes. These are third-party wheels, not on PyPI or piwheels.

Packages.gz files at http://archive.raspberrypi.com/debian/dists/{bookworm,trixie}/main/binary-{armhf,arm64}/. Bookworm, both arches: liblgpio1 and python3-lgpio 0.2.2-1~rpt1, python3-gpiozero 2.0.1-0+rpt1. Trixie, both arches: 0.2.2-1~rpt1+trixie and 2.0.1-0+rpt1+trixie. Image lists 2026-10-06-raspios-trixie-{arm64,armhf}-lite.info: python3-gpiozero 2.0.1-0+rpt1+trixie, python3-lgpio and liblgpio1 0.2.2-1~rpt1+trixie, python3-libgpiod 2.2.1-2+deb13u1 (armhf: 2.2.1-2+rpi1+deb13u1), python3-venv 3.13.5-1, python3.13 3.13.5-2+deb13u5. build-essential 12.12 is also preinstalled. Debian, per https://qa.debian.org/madison.php: python3-gpiozero is 1.6.2-1+b1 in bookworm and trixie. Debian has no python3-lgpio, liblgpio1 or lgpio package. Minor caveat: Debian forky and sid already carry python3-gpiozero 2.0.1-0.1, so 'Debian only has 1.6.2' holds for the stable releases only.

verdicts.corrected_claim: On a glibc-based python:3.12-slim image (bookworm or trixie; not Alpine/musl), every dependency installs from PyPI wheels on linux/arm/v7 and linux/arm64, so nothing compiles, even under QEMU. lgpio's cp312 wheels are statically linked: they need only libc and GLIBC_2.34. websockets 17.2 has cp312 manylinux armv7l and aarch64 wheels. For Python 3.13+ there are four ways to get lgpio: (a) compile it in a builder stage with swig, gcc and Python headers, using PYPI=1 for a self-contained module; (b) arm64 only: Adafruit's third-party static cp313–cp315 aarch64 wheels via --find-links; (c) arm/v7 only: piwheels' cp313 wheel plus Raspberry Pi's liblgpio1 installed in the image; (d) a Debian trixie image with Raspberry Pi's apt repo, using Debian's system python3.13 with python3-lgpio and python3-gpiozero, not the python:3.13 image's own interpreter.
verdicts.evidence: I downloaded lgpio-0.2.2.0-cp312-cp312-linux_armv7l.whl and -manylinux_2_34_aarch64.whl from PyPI and ran readelf -d on _lgpio*.so. The only NEEDED entries are libc.so.6 (and ld-linux-armhf.so.3 on armv7l). The highest symbol version is GLIBC_2.34, which python:3.12-slim-bookworm (glibc 2.36) and -trixie meet. https://pypi.org/pypi/websockets/json: websockets-17.2-cp312-cp312-manylinux2014_armv7l...manylinux_2_31_armv7l.whl and ...manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl exist. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docker-library/official-images/master/library/python: 'Tags: 3.12.15-slim-trixie, 3.12-slim-trixie, 3.12.15-slim, 3.12-slim' with Architectures amd64, arm32v5, arm32v7, arm64v8, ...; '3.12-slim-bookworm' with amd64, arm32v7, arm64v8, i386, ppc64le. The Python 3.13 options come from IMG-06 (Adafruit repo, piwheels apt_dependencies liblgpio1) and from lgpio's setup.py. Note: lgpio's armv7 wheel uses the plain linux_armv7l tag. That is fine for pip on armv7l, but I did not test it on hardware or under QEMU.

https://qa.debian.org/madison.php?package=python3-defaults+python3.13+python3.11: python3-defaults is 3.11.2-1 in bookworm and 3.13.5-1 in trixie. python3.13 is 3.13.5-2+deb13u5 in trixie (3.13.5-2+deb13u4 in trixie-updates). python3.11 is 3.11.2-6+deb12u8 in bookworm (deb12u9 in bookworm-security). The 2026-10-06 Lite .info files list python3 3.13.5-1 and python3.13 3.13.5-2+deb13u5 for both arm64 and armhf (Raspbian).

https://downloads.raspberrypi.com/os_list_imagingutility_v4.json, parsed. 'Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) | A port of Debian Trixie with the Raspberry Pi Desktop (Recommended)' has devices pi5-64bit, pi4-64bit, pi3-64bit and rel=2026-10-06. 'Raspberry Pi OS (32-bit)' (Trixie) and 'Lite (32-bit)' have pi5/pi4/pi3/pi2/pi1-32bit. 'Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) | A port of Debian Trixie with no desktop environment (Compatible with Raspberry Pi 3/4/400/5)'. Legacy Bookworm 32-bit and 64-bit (desktop, Lite, Full) entries are all dated 2026-10-06. In the imager.devices list, both 'Raspberry Pi 3' and 'Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W' have tags ['pi3-64bit','pi3-32bit']. Docs source documentation/asciidoc/computers/getting-started/install.adoc line 57: 'the recommended OS for your Raspberry Pi model is at the top of the list'.

The quote is verbatim from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/Documentation/userspace-api/gpio/gpio-v2-get-line-ioctl.rst lines 44-47. Raspberry Pi kernels go further: the line keeps its last driven level by default, so the heater does not merely 'can stay' on, it will. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/linux/rpi-6.18.y/drivers/pinctrl/bcm/pinctrl-bcm2835.c (Pi 3/4) has 'static bool persist_gpio_outputs = true; module_param(persist_gpio_outputs, bool, 0444); MODULE_PARM_DESC(... "Enable GPIO_OUT persistence when pin is freed")', and its free path has 'if (persist_gpio_outputs && fsel == BCM2835_FSEL_GPIO_OUT) return 0;' before '/* disable by setting to GPIO_IN */'. drivers/pinctrl/pinctrl-rp1.c (Pi 5) has 'persist_gpio_outputs = true' (0644) and '/* Return all pins to GPIO_IN, unless persist_gpio_outputs is set */'. So after a crash or kill -9 closes the fd, an output stays an output at its last level on Pi 3, 4 and 5 with stock kernels. The active-low heater line stays LOW, which means heater ON, until something else drives it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/documentation/master/documentation/asciidoc/computers/config_txt/gpio.adoc has the 'gpio=12=op,dh' example ('Set GPIO12 to be an output set to 1') and the comma-list syntax ('gpio=18,20=pu'), so 'gpio=22,23=op,dh' is valid. Verbatim: 'GPIO changes made through this mechanism do not have any direct effect on the kernel... they can be overridden by pinctrl entries in the Device Tree as well as utilities like pinctrl.' and 'there is a delay of a few seconds between power being applied and the changes taking effect – longer if booting over the network or from a USB mass storage device.' Caveat for the power-on window: Raspberry Pi engineer PhilE wrote on 2026-02-10 (https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=396148): 'On all Raspberry Pi SoCs, GPIOs 0-8 pull high at power on and GPIOs 9-27 pull low', and this 'cannot be altered'. So BCM 22/23 are weakly pulled toward the relays' ACTIVE level until the firmware applies gpio=. The same file notes that enable_jtag_gpio=1 takes over GPIO22-27, so it must stay unset. I found no primary source on whether the timing differs on Pi 5 (RP1).

verdicts.corrected_claim: The host-side reset tools are preinstalled on the Trixie Lite images (armhf and arm64, 2026-10-06): /usr/bin/pinctrl from raspi-utils-core 20260626-1, and the gpiod 2.2.1 CLI tools (libgpiod v2). For NFR-003 the reset must run on the host, as a Quadlet [Service] ExecStopPost or as ExecStopPost in a systemd unit that wraps `docker run`, because nothing inside a container runs once the container itself is killed, OOM-killed or stopped by the daemon. An init or wrapper process inside the container could still reset GPIO after the app process alone crashes, but that is not enough on its own. Use `pinctrl set 22,23 op dh`, which writes the pin registers so the level persists after pinctrl exits. Do not use plain gpioset: in v2 it holds the lines until it exits and blocks by default, so without -t0 it hangs ExecStopPost until the stop timeout, and its own help says the line state is not guaranteed after it exits. ExecStopPost runs as the unit's User=, so a non-root unit needs GPIO device access for the reset or a '+' prefix.
verdicts.evidence: http://archive.raspberrypi.com/debian/dists/trixie/main/Contents-arm64.gz: 'usr/bin/pinctrl  utils/raspi-utils-core'. 2026-10-06-raspios-trixie-{arm64,armhf}-lite.info: raspi-utils-core 20260626-1; gpiod and libgpiod3 2.2.1-2+deb13u1 (armhf: 2.2.1-2+rpi1+deb13u1). Bookworm's RPi repo has raspi-utils-core 20251002-1~bookworm. libgpiod v2.2.x tools/gpioset.c (https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/libs/libgpiod/libgpiod.git/plain/tools/gpioset.c?h=v2.2.x) help text: 'The line output state is maintained until the process exits', '-t ... If the last period is 0 then gpioset exits else the sequence repeats', 'It should not be assumed that a line will retain its state after gpioset exits. When a process exits, any GPIO lines it has requested are automatically released.' On stock Pi kernels the level does persist in practice (persist_gpio_outputs, see SAFE-01). The kernel uAPI returns EBUSY for a line already in use, so a gpioset-based reset fails while any process, such as a still-running container, holds the line. The User=/'+' behaviour of ExecStopPost is standard systemd semantics. I did not re-verify it or the /dev/gpiomem group permissions here.

verdicts.corrected_claim: lgpio creates a notification FIFO <workdir>/.lgd-nfy<N> as soon as the Python module is imported (module-level _callback_thread). The work dir is $LG_WD if set, otherwise the current directory. /tmp is used only if getcwd() fails, NOT when the current directory is unwritable. lgpio also chdir()s the whole process into that directory. gpiozero issue #1106 (open, opened 2024-01-09) shows the failure when run from an unwritable cwd ('Can't set permissions (436) for //.lgd-nfy0', then gpiozero 'Falling back from lgpio...'). systemd system services default to WorkingDirectory=/ and containers default to WORKDIR /. So every non-root unit or container must set LG_WD or WorkingDirectory/WORKDIR to a writable directory, not only hardened or read-only ones.
verdicts.evidence: lgpio-0.2.2.0 sdist: src/lgpio.h '#define LG_WD "LG_WD"  /* working directory */'. src/lgUtil.c lguGetWorkDir(): 'dirStr = getenv(LG_WD); if (dirStr) xSetWorkDir(dirStr); else { if (getcwd(xWorkDir, LG_MAX_PATH) == NULL) strcpy(xWorkDir, "/tmp"); } if (chdir(xWorkDir) < 0) ...'. src/lgNotify.c: 'snprintf(name, ..., "%s/.lgd-nfy%d", lguGetWorkDir(), handle); xCreatePipe(name, 0664);'. xCreatePipe does unlink, mkfifo, chmod and logs "Can't set permissions (%d) for %s, %m". lgpio_extra.py line 331 runs '_notify_thread = _callback_thread()' at import, and that class opens '.lgd-nfy{}' by relative path. https://github.com/gpiozero/gpiozero/issues/1106 'Scripts don't work if user doesn't have write permission to CWD' (opened 2024-01-09, open): 'Can't set permissions (436) for //.lgd-nfy0, No such file or directory', 'Falling back from lgpio: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '.lgd-nfy-3'', then 'RuntimeError: Cannot determine SOC peripheral base address'. systemd.exec(5) (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/main/man/systemd.exec.xml): WorkingDirectory= 'If not set, defaults to the root directory when systemd is running as a system instance'.

missed: Raspberry Pi kernels deliberately keep GPIO outputs driven after the line is released: persist_gpio_outputs=true by default in pinctrl-bcm2835 (Pi 3/4, parameter mode 0444, so it can only be changed at boot) and pinctrl-rp1 (Pi 5). After any crash the heater relay stays at its last level, ON if it was heating, in every deployment mode. Only an external reset (ExecStopPost) or a hardware watchdog fixes this, and the reset must actively drive BCM 22/23 HIGH. Releasing the pins to input is not enough.

At power-on, BCM 9-27 are pulled LOW on all Pi SoCs and this 'cannot be altered' (PhilE, 2026-02-10). So BCM 22/23 sit weakly at the ACTIVE level of the active-low relays for the few seconds before the firmware applies config.txt gpio=, and longer when booting from USB or network. Whether a relay closes then depends on the relay board. Only hardware (pull-ups on the relay inputs, or relay boards that stay off with a weak pull-down) closes this window. No deployment mode can.

For the ExecStopPost reset, use `pinctrl set 22,23 op dh` (raspi-utils-core, preinstalled). It writes the registers directly, so the level persists. libgpiod v2 `gpioset` blocks until killed unless given -t0, says the state is not guaranteed after it exits, and gets EBUSY if any process, such as a container that is still alive after its `docker run` client died, still holds the line. ExecStopPost runs as the unit's User=, so a non-root service (NFR-024) needs GPIO device access for the reset command or the '+' prefix.

piwheels' lgpio cp313 wheels need the system library liblgpio1 (apt_dependencies). They work in a native venv on 32-bit Pi OS Trixie, where liblgpio1 is preinstalled, but a python:3.13 arm/v7 container must also install Raspberry Pi's liblgpio1. The PyPI cp39-cp312 wheels are self-contained but need glibc >= 2.34, so no Alpine/musl base.

Third-party static lgpio wheels for cp313–cp315 aarch64 exist (adafruit/lgpio-python-wheels, via --find-links). This removes the need to compile on 64-bit Python 3.13+, but brings in a supply-chain dependency outside PyPI and piwheels.

Native deployment on Pi OS Trixie needs no compiling and no wheels for GPIO: python3-lgpio 0.2.2 and python3-gpiozero 2.0.1 are preinstalled on both the armhf and arm64 Lite images. A venv created with --system-site-packages, plus pure-Python wheels for the rest, works on both architectures. This makes the build simpler for native than for container modes.

lgpio chdir()s the whole process into LG_WD (or keeps the cwd) when it is imported. The app must not rely on relative paths for config or recipes after importing gpiozero/lgpio. Set GPIOZERO_PIN_FACTORY=lgpio explicitly, so that an lgpio failure (e.g. an unwritable work dir) fails hard instead of gpiozero silently trying other pin factories (#1106 shows the fallback chain).
